short: New Zealand has no AI act. Its AI Strategy of July 2025 takes a light-touch, principles-based approach relying on existing law; the Privacy Act 2020 binds, with fines of up to NZD 10,000 for its offences.
title: New Zealand AI Laws
subtitle: No AI act: a light-touch strategy that relies on existing law
body_html:
Status at a glance

No AI act, by choice. New Zealand's Strategy for Artificial Intelligence, published by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment in July 2025, takes "a light-touch and principles-based approach" and says it does not require additional regulatory overlay beyond existing law. AI is therefore governed by the Privacy Act 2020, consumer law and human rights law. Verified on 25 October 2026 against MBIE and the Office of the Privacy Commissioner.

Key instruments

InstrumentNumberDateLegal force
New Zealand's Strategy for Artificial Intelligence: Investing with confidenceMBIE, ISBN 978-1-991316-78-3July 2025Policy
Privacy Act 2020In force 1 December 2020; new IPP 3A (Privacy Amendment Act 2025) from 1 May 2026Binding

Who regulates and enforces

  • Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE): the AI strategy and responsible AI guidance for businesses.
  • Office of the Privacy Commissioner: the Privacy Act 2020.

Scope and reach

No AI-specific scope. Existing law applies to AI as it applies to any other activity.

Core obligations

  • None specific to AI. The Information Privacy Principles of the Privacy Act 2020 bind AI that handles personal information.

Penalties

BreachMaximumProvisionEnforcer
Privacy Act offences, including failing to notify a notifiable privacy breachA fine of up to NZD 10,000Privacy Act 2020, ss. 118 and 212, as the Privacy Commissioner's prosecution policy states itOffice of the Privacy Commissioner; courts

What is coming next

No government AI bill has been announced. The member's deepfake bill awaits its second reading, and Parliament's bills page for it is now the weekly watch. MBIE's news page still could not be read.

The deepfake bill, and the privacy layer in practice

The one AI-specific bill before Parliament is a member's bill, not a government one. ACT MP Laura McClure's Deepfake Digital Harm and Exploitation Bill, Bill 213-1 of the 54th Parliament, was drawn from the ballot in October 2025 and passed its first reading unanimously on 19 May 2026. It amends the Crimes Act 1961 and the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2015 so that an "intimate visual recording" includes an image or video manipulated by AI to depict a person without consent, criminalising the creation, sharing and threatened sharing of sexualised deepfakes. The Social Services and Community Committee took public submissions until 19 June 2026; at a hearing on 22 July 2026 McClure called the bill a first step and asked MPs to consider wider revision of digital-communication law and possible AI regulation. Parliament's bills site showed the bill awaiting its second reading when checked. No fine or sentence is stated here because the bill's text was not read.

The privacy layer has moved too. The Privacy Amendment Act 2025 received royal assent on 1 June 2025 and its new Information Privacy Principle 3A, in force from 1 May 2026, requires an agency to notify a person when it collects their personal information indirectly, from a third party, a broker or by scraping public sources, which reaches most AI training and enrichment pipelines. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner also issued the Biometric Processing Privacy Code 2025, the first sector code aimed at facial recognition and similar systems; retailer Bunnings has said its facial recognition trial was designed to comply with both the Act and the code. The Commissioner signed a joint international statement on AI and privacy harms in February 2026.

So the practical rulebook for AI in New Zealand is: the thirteen Information Privacy Principles plus IPP 3A, the biometrics code where faces or voices are processed, mandatory breach reporting, and, once the deepfake bill passes, criminal exposure for non-consensual intimate deepfakes. The July 2025 strategy's light-touch stance governs only whether a horizontal AI act will be written; it does not soften any of the above.

4 November 2026, against the sources above. The deepfake bill's first reading date and submission deadline are as RNZ and the sponsoring party report them, with the bill's stage read on Parliament's bills site; the bill text itself was not read. The biometrics code and the Bunnings statement are as the Equal Justice Project reports them.
